Consider the linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf T] with matrix representation [MATH: T,] given by [MATH: [2|0; 0|0]]

A triangle [MATH: S] has vertices at [MATH: (-1,2), (0,1)] and [MATH: (1,1).] Which of the following are coordinates of the vertices of [MATH: S',] the image of [MATH: S] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf T?]

  2. [MATH: (0,0)]

  3. [MATH: (2,0)]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To find the image of [MATH: S] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf T], we first create a matrix [MATH: X] containing all of the vertices of [MATH: S\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: [− 1|0|1; 2|1|1]]

Now, we compute the image of [MATH: X] under [MATH: \mathbf T] by calculating the matrix product [MATH: TX\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: TX|= [2|0; 0|0][− 1|0|1; 2|1|1]; = [− 2|0|2; 0|0|0]]

Therefore, the coordinates of the respective vertices of [MATH: S'] are [MATH: (-2,0),] [MATH: (0,0),] and [MATH: (2,0).]

So, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

sections.normalized_html:
• Case where [MATH: T] is non-singular:

    Let [MATH: \mathbf T] be the linear transformation with the following matrix representation: [MATH: [0|1; 1|2]] We can easily check that [MATH: T] is non-singular by computing its determinant: [MATH: det(T)|=|0|1; 1|2|; = 2 ⋅ 0 − 1 ⋅ 1; = − 1] To find the image of [MATH: \mathcal P] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf T], we create a matrix [MATH: X] containing all of the vertices of [MATH: \mathcal P] and then compute the product [MATH: TX{:}] [MATH: TX|= [0|1; 1|2][0|2|2; 1|0|1]; = [1|0|1; 2|2|4]] Therefore, the image of [MATH: \mathcal P] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is a triangle.
sections.readable_text:
- Case where [MATH: T] is non-singular:

Let [MATH: \mathbf T] be the linear transformation with the following matrix representation:
[MATH: [0|1; 1|2]]
We can easily check that [MATH: T] is non-singular by computing its determinant:
[MATH: det(T)|=|0|1; 1|2|; = 2 ⋅ 0 − 1 ⋅ 1; = − 1]
To find the image of [MATH: \mathcal P] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf T], we create a matrix [MATH: X] containing all of the vertices of [MATH: \mathcal P] and then compute the product [MATH: TX{:}]
[MATH: TX|= [0|1; 1|2][0|2|2; 1|0|1]; = [1|0|1; 2|2|4]]
Therefore, the image of [MATH: \mathcal P] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is a triangle.

[IMG: /graphics/b95ce660f76f3cb28bf70c9af98ae9fe]

sections.normalized_html:
• Case where [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is singular and has at least one nonzero entry:

    Let [MATH: \mathbf T] be the linear transformation with the following matrix representation: [MATH: [2|6; 1|3]] We can easily check that [MATH: T] is singular by computing its determinant: [MATH: det(T)|=|2|6; 1|3|; = 2 ⋅ 3 − 6 ⋅ 1; = 0] Now, computing the image of [MATH: \mathcal P] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf T,] we get [MATH: TX|= [2|6; 1|3][0|2|2; 1|0|1]; = [6|4|10; 3|2|5].] Consequently, the image of [MATH: \mathcal P] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is a line segment.

  • Case where [MATH: T] is the zero matrix:

    Let [MATH: \mathbf T] be the linear transformation represented by the zero matrix: [MATH: [0|0; 0|0]] Clearly, [MATH: T] is singular. Now, computing the image of [MATH: \mathcal P] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf T], we get [MATH: TX|= [0|0; 0|0][0|2|2; 1|0|1]; = [0|0|0; 0|0|0].] Therefore, the coordinates of the image's vertices are all [MATH: (0,0)], the origin [MATH: O] of the coordinate system.

items.readable_text:
Content:
Given a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf T] with an associated [MATH: 2\times 2] matrix [MATH: T,] there are three possibilities regarding the type of object formed under the action of [MATH: \mathbf{T}] by a two-dimensional preimage.

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the three-sided polygon [MATH: \mathcal P] with vertices [MATH: (0,1)], [MATH: (2,0)] and [MATH: (2,1),] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ae508c15cb767d68db89d7463f09a17f]

Content:
Let's describe the three possible types of object formed by the image of [MATH: \mathcal P{:}]

Content:
- Case where [MATH: T] is non-singular:

Let [MATH: \mathbf T] be the linear transformation with the following matrix representation:
[MATH: [0|1; 1|2]]
We can easily check that [MATH: T] is non-singular by computing its determinant:
[MATH: det(T)|=|0|1; 1|2|; = 2 ⋅ 0 − 1 ⋅ 1; = − 1]
To find the image of [MATH: \mathcal P] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf T], we create a matrix [MATH: X] containing all of the vertices of [MATH: \mathcal P] and then compute the product [MATH: TX{:}]
[MATH: TX|= [0|1; 1|2][0|2|2; 1|0|1]; = [1|0|1; 2|2|4]]
Therefore, the image of [MATH: \mathcal P] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is a triangle.

[IMG: /graphics/b95ce660f76f3cb28bf70c9af98ae9fe]

Content:

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the triangle below with vertices [MATH: (0,0),] [MATH: (2,1)] and [MATH: (2,3).]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/99fccef4611b8fcb6b3961cf37d73e71]

Content:
What is the image of this triangle under the action of the transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}] represented by the matrix
[MATH: [1|0; 0|0]]

Content:
To find the image of the triangle under the action of [MATH: \mathbf T,] we first create a matrix [MATH: X] containing all vertices of our triangle written as columns:

Content:
[MATH: [0|2|2; 0|1|3]]

Content:
Now, we compute the image of [MATH: X] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf T] by calculating the matrix product [MATH: TX\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: TX|= [1|0; 0|0][0|2|2; 0|1|3]; = [0|2|2; 0|0|0]]

Content:
Therefore, the coordinates of the image's vertices are [MATH: (0,0),] [MATH: (2,0),] [MATH: (2,0).] Notice that these points lie on the same line. Two of them even coincide!

Content:
So, the image of our triangle under the action of [MATH: \mathbf T] is the following line segment:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/942c0ed880bd56c0318d7fbf0588981e]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- Recall that for any linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf T] and region [MATH: D,] we have
[MATH: \text{Area}(\mathbf{T}(D)) = |\det(T)| \cdot \text{Area}(D).]
Since [MATH: |\det(T)| = 0] in this case, any object applied to [MATH: \mathbf T] collapses to an object with zero area.
- Also, the fact that [MATH: |\det(T)| = 0] tells us that [MATH: \mathbf T] has no inverse transformation. Therefore, it is impossible to recover the original triangle knowing only its image and the matrix [MATH: T.]

Item 2 — Example: Calculating the Coordinates of an Image Formed by a Singular Transformation

2. [MATH: (0,0)]
3. [MATH: (2,0)]

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To find the image of [MATH: S] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf T], we first create a matrix [MATH: X] containing all of the vertices of [MATH: S\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: [− 1|0|1; 2|1|1]]

Now, we compute the image of [MATH: X] under [MATH: \mathbf T] by calculating the matrix product [MATH: TX\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: TX|= [2|0; 0|0][− 1|0|1; 2|1|1]; = [− 2|0|2; 0|0|0]]

Therefore, the coordinates of the respective vertices of [MATH: S'] are [MATH: (-2,0),] [MATH: (0,0),] and [MATH: (2,0).]

So, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

Item 8 — Tutorial: Image Types Formed by Linear Transformations

Content:
Given a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf T] with an associated [MATH: 2\times 2] matrix [MATH: T,] there are three possibilities regarding the type of object formed under the action of [MATH: \mathbf{T}] by a two-dimensional preimage.

[IMG: /graphics/ae508c15cb767d68db89d7463f09a17f]

[MATH: [0|1; 1|2]]

[MATH: det(T)|=|0|1; 1|2|; = 2 ⋅ 0 − 1 ⋅ 1; = − 1]

[MATH: TX|= [0|1; 1|2][0|2|2; 1|0|1]; = [1|0|1; 2|2|4]]
Therefore, the image of [MATH: \mathcal P] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is a triangle.

[IMG: /graphics/b95ce660f76f3cb28bf70c9af98ae9fe]

[MATH: det(T)|=|2|6; 1|3|; = 2 ⋅ 3 − 6 ⋅ 1; = 0]
Now, computing the image of [MATH: \mathcal P] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf T,] we get

Consequently, the image of [MATH: \mathcal P] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is a line segment.

[IMG: /graphics/2de537c0c5f9e5bf868067dcd8dcbdb7]
- Case where [MATH: T] is the zero matrix:

Let [MATH: \mathbf T] be the linear transformation represented by the zero matrix:
[MATH: [0|0; 0|0]]
Clearly, [MATH: T] is singular. Now, computing the image of [MATH: \mathcal P] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf T], we get
[MATH: TX|= [0|0; 0|0][0|2|2; 1|0|1]; = [0|0|0; 0|0|0].]
Therefore, the coordinates of the image's vertices are all [MATH: (0,0)], the origin [MATH: O] of the coordinate system.

[IMG: /graphics/9b0cfda3c64dd9acf06c0c9b5ceb6c0e]
